extracted.intended_audience: general public interested in addiction, public health, and opioid policy
extracted.subtask_description: A consumer-facing explanatory blog post describing how Purdue Pharma and the Sackler family contributed to the U.S. opioid epidemic, including marketing tactics, physician influence, legal outcomes, and public-health impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing strategy targeting chronic non-malignant pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Purdue Pharma’s marketing strategy aimed to target the drug to all patients with chronic pain, not just cancer patients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Email from sales and marketing executive Michael Friedman: “Our current MS Contin business has created ‘a franchise’ with certain physicians who routinely write prescriptions for the drug…may be the bridge that we can use to expand the use of OxyContin beyond cancer patients to chronic non-malignant pain.” Sales grew from $48 million in 1996 to almost $1.1 billion in 2000.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using physicians and educational events to expand prescriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Purdue incorporated physicians into promotional efforts (dinners, weekend meetings) to increase prescribing of OxyContin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Company-run dinner programs and weekend meetings were used to influence prescribing; Richard Sackler noted physicians who attended wrote more than double the number of new Rxs, with weekend meetings increasing new prescriptions by a factor between 2.16 and 2.62.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial relationships with physicians and researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: Purdue and other companies provided funding to physicians and researchers, creating potential conflicts of interest that affected published research and clinical opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: neurologist Russell Portenoy’s pain center received millions from Purdue and others; Portenoy later admitted to financial relationships with over a dozen companies. The article notes research published in medical journals 'that lacked credibility' due to these ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spreading misinformation that minimized addiction risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Messaging and sponsored research falsely portrayed opioids as safe and effective and downplayed addiction risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states 'the spread of misinformation began stating that opioids are safe and effective.' Portenoy is quoted saying 'the risks of addiction to opioids were minimal,' and internal communications sought presentations arguing controlled-release products were less prone to addiction than immediate-release products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressive sales culture and explicit sales priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal company directives prioritized selling OxyContin aggressively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memo to Purdue’s sales team: 'Your priority is to Sell, Sell, Sell OxyContin.' This is presented alongside descriptions of sales tactics (dinners, meetings) that increased prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal deception, criminal plea, and civil settlements
rubrics_metrics.description: Purdue pleaded guilty to misleading the public about OxyContin’s addiction risk and faced numerous lawsuits leading to large settlements and bankruptcy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 2007 guilty plea with $600 million payment; continued lawsuits; early 2019 deal for the Sackler family to pay $3 billion and give up ownership; September 2019 bankruptcy filing that stayed litigation temporarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alleged asset shielding and family-level liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that Sackler family members moved or protected assets as litigation approached, prompting lawsuits aimed at the family as well as the company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New York attorney general tracked $1 billion in wire transfers suggesting the family tried to shield wealth. Transfers often went through Swiss bank accounts; the family has been investigated by the FBI over decades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactic of shifting blame to people with addiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Company leadership communications advocated attacking and blaming 'abusers' as a strategy to deflect responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted 2001 Richard Sackler email: 'We have to hammer on the abusers in every way possible. They are the culprits and the problem. They are reckless criminals.' Presented as an example of rhetoric used to shift blame onto addicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory and institutional failures or complicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions about regulatory agencies' roles, including alleged refusal to restrict OxyContin dispensing despite DEA requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article notes suspicion that the FDA may have been involved after refusing to place dispensing restrictions on OxyContin following DEA requests, indicating possible regulatory failure or complicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epidemiological and prescription metrics documenting harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistics used to quantify the scope of the opioid epidemic and the harms linked to prescription opioids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: 'An estimated 130 people die every day from overdosing on opioids'; in 2017 over 191 million opioid prescriptions dispensed; 21–29% of patients prescribed opioids for chronic pain misuse them; 8–12% develop an opioid use disorder; 80% of people who use heroin first misused a prescription opioid. These metrics are presented as evidence of public-health impact.
